status: drafted directly per the established Bible Character Index methodology (single-pass, not multi-agent workflow), corrected after adversarial fact-check, pending user read-through and confirmation
notes: 2 Corinthians is Paul's most autobiographical letter, and the tier structure reflects that directly: rather than treating his suffering, his defense of his apostleship, and his "thorn in the flesh" as generic doctrine, Paul himself gets a full person-type manager tier ("The Earthen Vessel," 4:7) carrying every personally-embodied narrative beat — the affliction in Asia (1:8-9), the catalogue of sufferings and the basket-escape from Damascus (11:23-33), the vision of paradise, the thorn/messenger-of-Satan episode (12:1-10), and his claim that "the signs of an apostle" were wrought among the Corinthians despite his refusal to be a financial burden to them (12:11-13). Titus is the book's other real character with narrative weight of his own — Paul's anxiety at not finding him in Troas (2:12-13), the comfort his arrival brought (7:6-7), and his role organizing the Jerusalem collection (8:6-23) — so he gets his own manager tier rather than being folded into Paul's. Everything else in the book is content-heavy teaching rather than character-driven scene, so it's modeled as seven law/theme tiers: comfort in affliction (1:3-7), the call to separation from unbelievers ("Touch Not the Unclean Thing," 6:14-7:1 — a doctrinally distinct unit sitting between Paul's catalogue of hardships and his appeal for open hearts, kept as its own tier rather than folded into the surrounding sections), the offender's discipline-and-restoration, the new covenant's unveiled glory, the ministry of reconciliation, the Jerusalem collection appeal, and the "false apostles"/"angels of light" polemic — the last of which now also carries chapter 10's material (the "weapons of our warfare," the "his letters are weighty... but his bodily presence is weak" criticism, and "he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord"), since chapter 10 is Paul's opening salvo against the same rival teachers chapters 11-13 go on to name explicitly as false apostles, not a separable topic. Each law tier is deliveredBy Paul as the letter's author. Two figures are deliberately NOT given person tiers despite carrying real weight in their sections: the unnamed offender (2:5-11, 7:8-12) is personally embodied (he sins, grieves, is restored) but the text never names him or gives him any other biographical data, and Paul's own point is the church's collective response to him, not his individual story — so he's a law tier, not a submanager or manager. Likewise "such are false apostles" (11:13) is a group the text does not individually differentiate by name, so per the collective-entry rule it's kept as one law tier rather than inventing individual profiles. The "brethren" sent with Titus (8:18, 8:22), by contrast, ARE individually distinguished by the text itself — one commended for renown "in the gospel throughout all the churches" and chosen by the churches for the collection journey (8:18-19), the other independently described as "oftentimes proved diligent in many things" and now even more so (8:22) — so, correcting an earlier over-compression, they are kept as two separate submanager entries rather than one collective entry; neither is named by the text, and any traditional guesses at their identity (e.g. Luke) are flagged as extra-biblical speculation, not asserted as fact. Timothy (co-sender, 1:1, 1:19) and Silvanus (1:19) are minor, loyalty-boost submanagers under Paul with zero independent narrative action in this specific book. A naming-variant flag (not a collision between two different people, but worth noting so it isn't mistaken for one): the Silvanus named here is the same man called "Silas" in Acts, just a different form of the same Latin/Greek name. The offender's identity is sometimes traditionally linked to the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5, but 2 Corinthians itself never makes that connection explicit, so it is flagged as an open, unresolved question rather than asserted as fact.

characters.name: Paul

verses.note: Opens the letter as 'an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God,' with Timothy, to the church at Corinth.
Describes trouble in Asia so severe he 'despaired even of life' and 'had the sentence of death' in himself.
Defends, under oath ('I call God for a record upon my soul'), why he changed his travel plans and did not yet return to Corinth.
'We have this treasure in earthen vessels' — troubled, perplexed, persecuted, cast down, but not destroyed; the book's central image for his own weakness carrying God's power.
Catalogues his ministry's hardships — stripes, imprisonments, tumults, labours, watchings, fastings.

The great autobiographical catalogue: five times forty stripes save one, thrice beaten with rods, once stoned, thrice shipwrecked, a night and a day in the deep, plus daily 'the care of all the churches.'
Escapes Damascus by being let down in a basket through a window in the city wall.
Recounts being 'caught up to the third heaven' into paradise and hearing 'unspeakable words.'
The thorn in the flesh, 'the messenger of Satan to buffet me' — three prayers for its removal answered with 'My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.'

Claims 'the signs of an apostle were wrought among you... in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds,' and asks forgiveness, half-ironically, for the one way he 'wronged' the Corinthians: refusing to be a financial burden to them.
Announces this will be his third visit to Corinth, warning he will not spare offenders this time.

funFacts: Scripture never states what the 'thorn in the flesh' actually was (12:7) — proposals (an eye ailment, a speech impediment, ongoing persecution) are all extra-biblical speculation, not textual fact.

The phrase 'the very chiefest apostles' (11:5; 12:11) is genuinely ambiguous in the text itself — it may be sarcastic shorthand for the rival false apostles at Corinth, or may refer to the original Twelve; 2 Corinthians does not clarify which.

characters.name: Titus

verses.note: Paul, given an open door at Troas, has 'no rest in my spirit' because he could not find Titus there, and departs for Macedonia.
'God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted us by the coming of Titus' — Titus's arrival and report bring Paul relief.
Titus's own spirit was 'refreshed' by the Corinthians, and his affection toward them 'is more abundant' remembering their obedience.
Titus had already begun organizing the Jerusalem collection among the Corinthians and is urged to finish it.
Titus accepts Paul's exhortation and, 'being more forward, of his own accord,' goes to Corinth himself.
Paul calls him 'my partner and fellowhelper concerning you.'
Paul recalls sending Titus (with 'a brother') to Corinth and defends that neither of them took advantage of the church.

funFacts: Titus's report from Corinth is the direct occasion for most of chapters 1-7's tone of relief and reconciliation — the letter's emotional turning point hinges on his arrival.

characters.name: Timothy
characters.perkNote: Named co-sender and travel companion; no independent action of his own within this specific book.

genealogy.mother: eunice — 2 Timothy 1:5, not indexed in this book

verses.note: Named alongside Paul as co-sender: 'Paul... and Timothy our brother.'
Named as one who, with Paul and Silvanus, preached Christ among the Corinthians.

characters.name: Silvanus
characters.perkNote: Naming-variant flag, not a collision: this is the same man called 'Silas' in the book of Acts, a different form of the same name, not a second person.

verses.note: Named with Paul and Timothy as one who preached the Son of God among the Corinthians.

characters.name: The Brother Renowned in the Gospel
characters.perkNote: Unnamed in the text. The text individually distinguishes this man from the second brother (8:22) by his own description, so — correcting an earlier draft that collapsed both into one collective entry — he is kept as his own submanager rather than merged. Some traditions guess his identity (e.g. Luke), but 2 Corinthians itself never names him, so no identity is asserted here.

verses.note: Described as the brother 'whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches,' and also chosen by the churches to travel with Paul administering the collection.
Called, together with the second brother, 'the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ.'

characters.name: The Brother Often Proved Diligent
characters.perkNote: Unnamed in the text. Individually distinguished from the first brother (8:18-19) by his own description — 'oftentimes proved diligent' — so kept as his own submanager rather than merged into a single collective entry.

verses.note: Described as 'our brother, whom we have oftentimes proved diligent in many things,' sent along with even greater confidence in the Corinthians.
Called, together with the first brother, 'the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ.'

characters.name: The God of All Comfort
characters.purpose: Opens the letter by naming God as 'the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort' who comforts believers in tribulation specifically so they can pass that comfort on to others in trouble — framing affliction as purposeful rather than meaningless.

verses.note: 'Blessed be God... the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble.'
'As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ.'

characters.name: Touch Not the Unclean Thing
characters.purpose: Instructs believers not to be 'unequally yoked together with unbelievers,' arguing that righteousness and unrighteousness, light and darkness, cannot genuinely partner together — and calls the church to come out and be separate, on the promise that God will then receive them as sons and daughters, and to perfect holiness out of reverence for God rather than mere rule-following.

verses.note: 'Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?'
'Come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you.'
'Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.'

characters.name: The Offender's Sorrow and Restoration
characters.purpose: Instructs the church on balancing discipline with restoration for a member who caused grief — the punishment already inflicted 'by many' is called sufficient, and the church is urged to forgive and comfort him so he isn't 'swallowed up with overmuch sorrow,' modeling godly sorrow that leads to repentance rather than despair.

verses.note: 'Sufficient to such a man is this punishment... forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow... confirm your love toward him.'
Paul does not regret the sorrow his earlier letter caused, since 'godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of.'

funFacts: The offender is never named in 2 Corinthians. He is sometimes traditionally linked to the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5, but the text of 2 Corinthians itself never makes that connection explicit — flagged here as an open, unresolved question, not asserted fact.

characters.name: The Veil Taken Away
characters.purpose: Contrasts the old covenant (the letter, given through Moses with a fading, veiled glory) with the new covenant of the Spirit, whose glory is unveiled and increasing — explaining why suffering apostles can still carry surpassing, unfading power that is 'of God, and not of us.'

verses.note: God 'hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.'
Recalls Moses putting a veil over his face, and states the veil 'is done away in Christ' — 'when it shall turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away.'
'We all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory.'
'God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.'

characters.name: Ambassadors for Christ
characters.purpose: Teaches the apostolic calling to carry God's message of reconciliation to the world — grounded in the hope of an eternal 'building of God' beyond the earthly body, the reality of standing before Christ's judgment seat, and the declaration that anyone in Christ is a new creature.

verses.note: Contrasts the earthly 'tabernacle' of the body with 'a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.'
'Willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.'
'We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.'
'If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.'
God has given 'the ministry of reconciliation,' and believers are declared 'ambassadors for Christ.'
'He hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.'

characters.name: The Cheerful Giver
characters.purpose: Appeals for the Corinthians to complete their promised gift for the Jerusalem church, using the Macedonian churches' generosity despite deep poverty as an example and Christ's own voluntary poverty as the ultimate model — insisting giving must come from a willing mind, not compulsion, since 'God loveth a cheerful giver.'

verses.note: The churches of Macedonia, out of 'deep poverty,' gave beyond their power, first giving 'their own selves to the Lord.'
'Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich' — Christ as the model for the appeal.
'If there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.'
'He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly... God loveth a cheerful giver.'
'Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.'

characters.name: Angels of Light
characters.purpose: Warns the Corinthian church against rival teachers preaching 'another Jesus' and commending themselves, exposing their self-commendation as counterfeit ministry — beginning in chapter 10 with Paul's declaration that the weapons of his warfare are not carnal but 'mighty through God' for pulling down strongholds and 'every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God,' and his answer to the charge that his letters are 'weighty and powerful' while his 'bodily presence is weak': that only the Lord's commendation counts, since 'he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.' Since even Satan can appear as 'an angel of light,' true apostleship is instead marked by suffering and weakness, not polished self-promotion.

verses.note: 'For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh... casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.'
Quotes the criticism against him: 'His letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.'
'He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.'
Warns against bearing with one who 'preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached.'
'Such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.'
'Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also be transformed as the ministers of righteousness.'
Paul's rhetorical self-comparison against them — 'Are they Hebrews? so am I... Are they ministers of Christ?... I am more.'

funFacts: This is a collective, unnamed group in the text — 2 Corinthians never names a single individual rival, so no invented individual profiles are created for them, per the collective-entry rule.

Chapter 10's warfare imagery and the 'weighty letters, weak presence' criticism are Paul's opening move in the same polemic that chapters 11-13 name explicitly as 'false apostles' — kept in one tier rather than split, since the text itself treats it as a single continuous argument.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

churchOfCorinth.note: The letter's addressee, 'the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints which are in all Achaia' — the recipient body, not an individual character.

churchesOfMacedonia.note: Referenced collectively as the example of generosity that opens the giving appeal; not individually named or differentiated by congregation.

unnamedOffenderTradition.note: A traditional (not textually confirmed) link between the offender disciplined here and the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 — 2 Corinthians itself never makes this connection explicit, so it is logged here as unresolved rather than merged into the offender's entry as fact.
